video_title: MacroVoices #559 Ole Hansen: What’s Next After The spec Washout in Commodities
gist: Saxo Bank's Ole Hansen argues the 77% collapse in hedge-fund commodity net length (vs only ~10% index retracement) is setting up a 2027 rebound, seeing copper's AI-driven selloff as a speculative flush, refined-product/diesel tightness as the real inflation driver, and Brent's post-war normal at $70-90. He stays bullish commodities for 2027 with a metals tilt, while the trade desk proposes a copper bull call spread and flags Nvidia's muted post-earnings reaction, a strong dollar and Fed hike risk.

themes.theme: Speculative washout and positioning as a contrarian setup

insights.claim: Ole Hansen says the combined hedge-fund net long across 25 major commodity futures collapsed 77% in roughly two months (COT data to Nov 10, 2026), back to early-year lows, while the Bloomberg Commodity Index retraced only about 10%.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Positioning has been flushed far more than prices, leaving fuel for a rebound once the trend turns.
insights.quote: we basically seen a 77% collapse in that length in the in the last two months alone

insights.claim: Hansen views the collapsed speculative positioning as a reverse indicator setting up the next commodity run higher, but expects patience is needed: likely not before year-end 2026, rather into 2027, and only once a technical or fundamental catalyst appears.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Contrarian accumulation window into 2027 rather than an immediate trade.
insights.quote: I don't think it's going to happen before a year end, but I think into next year then uh this is the setup the market needs for for a rebound.

insights.claim: Hansen, a former hedge-fund employee, frames trend-following funds as buying strength and selling weakness via moving-average crossover signals, so current short/medium/long-term MA signals pointing lower are driving funds to cut longs and add shorts.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Spec flows are mechanical; price stabilization flips the signals and the flow.
insights.quote: they buy into strength and sell into weakness and right now we are seeing weakness so they're selling into that weakness in order to follow the trend

insights.claim: Hansen expects the catalyst for a commodity rebound to be inflation rolling over and the focus on rate hikes diminishing, especially if growth weakens enough that the Fed must weigh its dual mandate.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Watch inflation prints as the trigger for spec re-entry into commodities.

insights.claim: In grains, speculative length in six soy and grain contracts surged from flat to about a million contracts during the July-August 2026 Black Sea/heat-wave scare and has now fallen back to almost flat, with corn flipping to net short from a record long and wheat net short as it has been for most of the last 4-4.5 years.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Ag positioning is washed out; downside selling pressure is largely exhausted.
insights.quote: Just in in the six soy and grains contracts alone, it jumped from being flat to a million contracts. And now we're basically literally back to almost back to flat.

insights.claim: Hansen says he is struggling to be bearish across the grain sector at current levels because liquidation is ending and catalysts like Russia-Ukraine or El Nino effects on the southern hemisphere could trigger a reversion.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Asymmetric long setup in grains after the spec flush.
insights.quote: So at these at these levels I'm struggling to be bearish in in across the grain sector.

insights.claim: Hansen notes agricultural markets have thinner liquidity than energy and metals, which amplifies speculative surges and collapses when several fundamentals align at once.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Expect bigger overshoots both ways in ags than in energy/metals.

insights.claim: Hansen thinks the current commodity super-cycle, which he labels energy transition and electrification and dates from the 2020 pandemic low (prices up about 150% since), is potentially only at its beginning, following the 1970s and 2000s China/India super-cycles.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Treat current drawdown as a correction within a multi-year bull, not the end.
insights.quote: Well, I think we potentially only at the beginning of it.

insights.claim: Hansen argues the cycle is underpinned by supply struggling to meet demand and by companies shifting from just-in-time to just-in-case inventory in a deglobalizing world, alongside structural themes like defense priorities.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Structural inventory-building demand supports a higher floor for commodity prices.

insights.claim: Hansen says commodities have returned about 25% year-to-date in 2026, much of it from energy and from extreme backwardation benefiting passive long-only returns, while metals and industrials face headwinds from rate hikes, a strong dollar, China, AI data-center and tariff worries.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Roll yield, not just price, has driven 2026 commodity returns.

insights.claim: Hansen maintains a bullish 2027 commodity outlook but expects returns below 2026's ~25% because energy will not repeat; he expects a recovery in metals and thinks commodities may do as well as equities, which he doubts will match prior years' returns.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Rotate commodity focus from energy toward metals for 2027; keep commodities as a diversifier.
insights.quote: So I'll be focusing on the uh on the metal sector

insights.claim: Hansen notes sector leadership rotates sharply year to year (precious metals +80% in 2025 then -14% in 2026; energy -10% in 2025 then strong in 2026), so investors without a strong sector view should hold broad commodity exposure.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Broad baskets avoid the timing risk of picking last year's winner.
insights.quote: If you want to be invested in commodities and you don't have a specific or strong view about an individual commodity or sector, then the broad approach makes sense.

insights.claim: Hansen argues commodities are spot-driven markets set by daily supply and demand, so they are unlikely to be the asset that responds most aggressively to a macro shock such as an AI capex bust, even if short-term spec positioning anticipates it.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Commodities should be less sensitive to an AI bust than equities beyond the short-term spec move.

themes.theme: AI capex fears versus electrification demand

insights.claim: Hansen says the AI capex bust fear is hitting commodities tied to power production such as copper and gas, but he sees the impact as mostly psychological and short-term because global electrification, EV adoption accelerated by high war-driven energy prices, and large ongoing AI projects continue.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Fade AI-driven commodity selloffs where supply remains constrained.
insights.quote: So I think the impact is more a psychological one here in the short term than an actual real one

insights.claim: Hansen observes some level of fossil-fuel demand destruction in China, driven by EV adoption and high energy prices, whose extent will only become clear once markets normalize.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Structural oil demand in China may be weaker than pre-war assumptions.

insights.claim: Patrick reports Nvidia beat earnings after a nearly 40% stock collapse but the stock gave back overnight gains in regular hours, which he reads as the AI-trade downside distribution not yet being played out, with the Anthropic IPO reception as the next sentiment test.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices co-host)
insights.so_what: Selling into good news signals the AI unwind is incomplete.
insights.quote: we're recording this before the anthropic IPO

insights.claim: Erik Townsend frames the equity market's central question as whether the AI capex boom ends and crumbles due to a shortage of private credit.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Private credit availability is the transmission channel for an AI bust.

themes.theme: Energy: Hormuz, backwardation and the refined-products squeeze

insights.claim: Hansen describes the Middle East situation as no war, no peace: the market already prices a 2027 crude surplus, but he believes no solution is possible without Iran on board because as long as Iran cannot export crude it will keep disrupting the region.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Crude pricing may be underestimating unresolved supply risk.
insights.quote: until Iran is being allowed to export it crude again, they will obviously continue to uh to create trouble

insights.claim: Hansen's initial guess is that if Brent traded $60-70 before the war, $70-90 will be the new normal after normalization, still with some backwardation adding to returns.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Higher structural oil floor; long-only still earns roll yield.
insights.quote: if Brent was trading 60 $70 range before the war then 70 to 90 is probably going to be the the new normal

insights.claim: Hansen stresses that inflation relief requires diesel (distillate) prices to fall, not crude, since consumers pay for refined fuels; distillates were still above $160 and gasoil one-year spreads showed prompt trading 25% above a year forward.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Track diesel cracks, not crude, as the inflation signal.
insights.quote: it doesn't really matter whether crude is trading 110 or 90 because that's what what feeds through to inflation is what we as consumers pay for fuel

insights.claim: Hansen says 2026 energy-sector total return was 74% versus about 45% from flat price alone, meaning extreme backwardation added roughly 30% in roll income, even though natural gas was down about 25% year-to-date.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Curve structure can matter as much as price direction for long-only investors.

insights.claim: Hansen calls natural gas a dog to trade from the long side because its curve is in about 24% contango, while metals are in roughly 5% funding-cost contango and sugar, coffee and soybeans show small backwardation.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Avoid long nat gas futures; roll costs erode returns.
insights.quote: that's why natural gas is just a a dog to trade from a long perspective because of the the contango

insights.claim: Hansen expects energy backwardation to persist into 2027 with a flatter curve but no shift to contango.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Energy roll yield remains positive but smaller next year.

insights.claim: Hansen says refined-product and LNG shipments remain below pre-war levels because of missing refinery capacity in Russia and roughly 10% missing in the Middle East, so refined products, especially distillates, will be the last to normalize after any settlement.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Refined-product tightness and inflation pressure outlast any peace deal.

insights.claim: Erik Townsend argues a new permanently high crack-spread regime is underappreciated: destroyed refineries take a decade to rebuild and no one wants to invest, so crack spreads stay high; Hansen agrees but has not done deep analysis.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Refiners/crack exposure may stay structurally profitable beyond the war.
insights.quote: you blew up a bunch of refineries and it takes a decade to build another one and nobody wants to invest the money to do it. So I think the crack spreads stay high pretty much permanently.

insights.claim: Hansen explains that refiners may cut runs despite high diesel cracks because gasoline cracks have collapsed to pre-war levels and a barrel yields only a fixed share of distillates, so much of the barrel is unprofitable; delayed maintenance from running flat out also constrains output.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: High diesel cracks alone may not bring more diesel supply.

insights.claim: Hansen says Europe was left exposed because aging refineries closed without permission or appetite to build new ones, increasing reliance on Middle East supply that was then cut off.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: European diesel remains most vulnerable to Gulf disruption.
insights.quote: In Europe, we uh we've been left a little bit naked once again.

insights.claim: Hansen flags open questions for post-war oil: demand destruction, whether OPEC discipline holds or a market-share battle erupts now that the UAE has left OPEC, and how much China rebuilds stockpiles.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: UAE exit from OPEC raises risk of a price-war scenario after normalization.

insights.claim: Patrick sees crude, after a 50% rise off June lows to about $105 and a 20% correction in three weeks, as asymmetric: maybe $5 more downside but a return to October highs if flows through Hormuz are disrupted, absent an imminent peace deal.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices co-host)
insights.so_what: Pullback in crude is a potential long entry with skewed upside.
insights.quote: maybe there's $5 of further downside volatility on oil, but if there's anything that uh disrupts the existing oil flows, we could easily find ourselves back to October highs

themes.theme: Metals: gold, silver, platinum and copper

insights.claim: Hansen says precious metals are a market you have to fall out of love with before it bottoms; the gold-and-silver sector is down 14% in 2026 after an 80% gain in 2025, which he sees as a natural correction.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Rising negativity in precious metals is a contrarian bottoming signal.
insights.quote: precious metals really is a mark where you you kind of have to fall out of love with it before it it finds a bottom

insights.claim: Hansen says gold's run from the 2022-23 triple bottom to the early-2026 peak was fueled by central banks, ETF investors and Chinese investors; leveraged hedge funds are now reducing positions, while ETF demand held up despite spiking real yields but is starting to roll over.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Fading ETF demand removes a key support; bottom may take time.

insights.claim: Hansen believes long-term gold drivers remain, notably rising US debt burdens concentrated at the front of the curve where rates have spiked most, which keeps investors seeking metals to sit outside the system.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Fiscal funding stress keeps the structural case for precious metals intact.
insights.quote: that will still be a driver for for investor appetite into methods as just in order to sit outside sit outside the system

insights.claim: Hansen is lukewarm on silver: down about a third in 2026, gold/silver ratio back above 81 from low 70s, potentially seeking support in the mid-$40s, with extreme volatility forcing holders out and high prices damaging industrial demand.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Silver's deficit narrative is outweighed by fading investor interest; wait for a low.
insights.quote: that's also why I'm I'm a bit lukewarm on on silver for now

insights.claim: Hansen notes platinum's break above $1,000 took out a 17-year downtrend, and five-year annualized returns are about 13% for silver and 15% for platinum, but he is not sure a low has been found.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Long-run returns are attractive once prices stabilize.

insights.claim: Hansen views copper's break below its 200-day moving average as a speculative flush tied to Nasdaq/AI weakness rather than a change in fundamentals, with the long-term electrification story and rising mining input costs intact.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Copper dip is a buying opportunity for long-term holders.
insights.quote: So I see this as more as a speculative flush out than any any change in the the underlying underlying fundamentals.

insights.claim: Hansen says over 1 million tons of exchange-monitored copper stocks exist, 67% held in COMEX warehouses in the US and much of the LME's 30% also stateside; if no US tariff is introduced, some could flow back to the global market and ease tightness elsewhere, while Chinese inventories are extremely low.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: US tariff decision is a key swing factor for ex-US copper tightness.

insights.claim: Hansen cites Goldman Sachs's 2027 outlook as bullish copper with two risks: AI and possible tariffs.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Consensus bull case hinges on AI and tariff outcomes.

insights.claim: Patrick proposes a tactical copper trade: a March 2027 COMEX copper $6.00/$6.25 bull call spread on options expiring Dec 28, costing about 6 cents for about 19 cents potential profit, with copper near $5.74 after a nearly 20% two-month drop.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices co-host)
insights.so_what: Defined-risk way to play a partial oversold bounce in copper.
insights.quote: The option structure is the $6 to $6.25 bull call spread at a net cost of approximately 6 cents per pound.

insights.claim: Patrick says large speculators were at the 100th percentile long in copper during a summer rounding top, so the breakdown is a shakeout, with the $5.25-5.75 March-lows zone as a tactical place for short-term lows; copper miners have also corrected sharply.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices co-host)
insights.so_what: Watch copper miners for opportunities alongside the metal.

insights.claim: Patrick sees gold in a distribution cycle since the August high, approaching $3,700, with $3,600 (50% retracement of the 2025 bull market) and $3,200 (summer 2025 consolidation) as key support where it may become a compelling buy.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices co-host)
insights.so_what: Defined levels for scaling into gold.

insights.claim: Hansen says the near-record El Nino has not spiked grain prices because global stockpiles, including rice, are ample and robust, but the coming months remain critical and could also hit energy production and mining via heat or flooding.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: El Nino risk is underpriced but buffered by stocks; watch next few months.
insights.quote: we're most certainly not out of the woods

insights.claim: Hansen is most concerned about sugar as the food commodity in the eye of the El Nino storm because supply depends on Brazil, India and Thailand and it already rallied strongly earlier in 2026.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: Sugar is the ag market most exposed to weather-driven upside.

themes.theme: Macro drivers: inflation, Fed, dollar and equities

insights.claim: Hansen says the latest CPI print shows inflation spreading beyond energy and becoming stickier, but any rollover would matter hugely because Fed chair Kevin Walsh was appointed to cut rates, not hike.
insights.speaker: Ole Hansen (Saxo Bank)
insights.so_what: An inflation rollover could rapidly flip Fed policy toward cuts, bullish for commodities.
insights.quote: the Federal Reserve has not been especially Kevin Walsh is not been employed to hike rates. It's been employed to cut rates

insights.claim: Patrick reports Waller has floated a 50bp hike for the December Fed meeting, with markets pricing about a 10% probability, and says AI credit-cycle carnage has not slowed the Fed's tightening ambitions.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices co-host)
insights.so_what: Fed tightening continues despite AI credit stress.

insights.claim: Patrick says the dollar index is approaching 104 with broad strength against the euro (toward 1.10), sterling, yen, CAD and AUD, signaling funding stress, and he sees a move toward 105 as plausible.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices co-host)
insights.so_what: Broad dollar strength is a headwind for commodities and signals funding stress.

insights.claim: Patrick says the S&P 500 is in a decisive distribution cycle below its 50-day moving average; even a rally to 7,500 would not turn it bullish, and 7,000-7,200 is a downside target zone, with VIX at 25-28 far below Liberation Day's 50+.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices co-host)
insights.so_what: Equity selling not yet capitulative; another ~5% downside possible before a Christmas rally.
